articles.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
articles.summary: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.
articles.content:
A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

An Anti-Aging Drug Shows Promise

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

The impact is broad and meaningful for the general public given the prevalence of Alzheimer's and the lack of effective early treatments. The article provides detailed context about the study, its findings, and implications, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news.

articles.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
articles.summary: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.
articles.content:
A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations.

The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons.

Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug.

The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions.

The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress.

"I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Why Scientists Are Taking a New Look at Psychedelics

Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood.

Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances.

In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function.

Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons.

This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions.

In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs."

Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed.

As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer.

Watching Psilocybin Rewire the Brain

To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy.

This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment.

Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate.

Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain.

Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines.

But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace.

Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections.

After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons.

Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood.

For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin.

"Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab.

"These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain."

Psilocybin Affects Healthy and Stressed Brains Differently

One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress.

In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level.

This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance.

The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress.

To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression.

Prolonged stress is known to interfere with neural communication and can cause substantial losses of synaptic connections. Over time, these changes can weaken the circuits involved in important brain functions.

When the stressed mice received psilocybin, the researchers observed an especially strong increase in the formation of new dendritic spines.

At the same time, psilocybin prevented the unusually high rate of connection loss associated with chronic stress.

Together, these effects suggest that psilocybin may do more than temporarily increase the number of connections in the brain. Under stressful conditions, it may also help preserve existing connections and restore circuitry that has been disrupted.

"These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain's underlying condition," Zuo added.

"This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders."

Could Psilocybin Rewire the Brain Without Hallucinations?

Perhaps the most significant implication of the research concerns a longstanding question in psychedelic medicine: Are hallucinations and altered states of consciousness necessary for the brain changes that might contribute to therapeutic benefits?

To explore this possibility, the scientists examined the role of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs), which are proteins on the surfaces of cells that respond to chemical signals. These receptors are central to the effects of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics.

The researchers focused on a group of nerve cells called Layer 5 pyramidal neurons. These cells are located in the cerebral cortex, the outer region of the brain involved in complex functions such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

Layer 5 pyramidal neurons serve as important communication pathways that send information from the cortex to other brain regions. They also contain high levels of serotonin 2A receptors, making them especially relevant to understanding psilocybin's effects.

Using genetically modified mice, the team selectively changed whether these neurons possessed the receptors.

The results revealed a striking separation between changes in brain connections and a behavior associated with psychedelic activity.

When the researchers restored serotonin 2A receptors only in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin was still able to stimulate the development of new synapses and help stabilize them.

Surprisingly, these mice did not display the characteristic head twitch response that researchers commonly use as an indicator of psychedelic activity in rodents.

The scientists then performed the opposite experiment.

When they removed serotonin 2A receptors specifically from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin lost its ability to stimulate the same structural growth of synapses.

However, the mice still exhibited the head twitch response.

These contrasting results demonstrate that serotonin 2A receptor signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for the structural brain changes observed in the experiments, while those same receptors are not required for the psychedelic-associated behavioral response.

In other words, the cellular pathway responsible for psilocybin's brain rewiring can be separated from the pathway responsible for this particular behavioral marker of psychedelic activity.

Because mice cannot describe subjective experiences, the head twitch response does not directly establish whether an animal is experiencing hallucinations. Nevertheless, the findings provide important evidence that these two effects involve distinct cellular mechanisms.

A Potential Path Toward Psychedelic Treatments Without the Trip

The discovery could have major implications for the development of future psychiatric medications.

If researchers can identify compounds that activate the brain's ability to rebuild and reorganize neural connections without triggering psychedelic effects, it may become possible to create treatments that preserve some of psilocybin's therapeutic potential while avoiding the need for patients to undergo intense altered states of consciousness.

Such medications could be easier to administer and might require less intensive clinical supervision than conventional psychedelic-assisted therapies.

"By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs," Zuo said.

"Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects -- making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population."

Although the results are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the same cellular mechanisms operate in humans and whether separating brain rewiring from psychedelic effects can produce effective treatments for depression, PTSD, or other psychiatric disorders.

For now, the findings provide a more detailed picture of how psilocybin changes the brain and reveal a potential strategy for harnessing its effects on neural connections without relying on the psychedelic experience itself.

The study's other UC Santa Cruz coauthors include molecular and cell biologists Jacob Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, and Ju Lu, alongside Zuo.

Funding came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging. The psilocybin used in the experiments was supplied through the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough showing how psilocybin rewires the brain to promote neuroplasticity, with potential to develop new psychiatric treatments that separate therapeutic benefits from psychedelic effects. This discovery could lead to safer, more accessible treatments for depression, PTSD, and other mental health disorders, impacting a broad population. The study is detailed and focused on a single important topic with clear real-world implications.

articles.title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11233-9In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
articles.content: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant medical breakthrough using CRISPR base editing to durably lower harmful lipid levels, which are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease. This single-dose gene editing treatment shows strong, lasting effects in animal models and has advanced to human clinical trials, indicating broad potential impact on public health by improving treatment for hyperlipidemia and reducing cardiovascular risk.
articles.personality_title: New Gene Editing Treatment Could Lower Bad Cholesterol with One Dose
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – High levels of bad cholesterol (LDL) and fats called triglycerides in the blood increase the risk of heart disease. Many people take medicine to lower these fats but often don’t reach the right levels.

**What happened** – Scientists used a gene-editing tool called CRISPR to change a gene named ANGPTL3 in the liver. They gave this treatment as a single injection using tiny particles to deliver the medicine safely. This method was tested in animals like mice and monkeys, where it successfully lowered bad cholesterol and triglycerides by almost half or more. The effect lasted for at least three years after just one treatment. This success has led to the start of human clinical trials.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows a one-time treatment can provide long-lasting control of harmful blood fats, unlike current medicines that must be taken regularly. Lowering ANGPTL3 reduces the main causes of heart disease, which could help many patients who don’t respond well to existing treatments.

**What’s next step** – Researchers are now testing this treatment in people with hard-to-treat high cholesterol. If it works safely in humans, it could become a new way to prevent heart disease by fixing the problem at the gene level with just one dose.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A single gene-editing treatment targeting ANGPTL3 has shown lasting ability to lower bad cholesterol and fats in animals and is now being tested in humans to fight heart disease risk.

articles.title: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
articles.summary: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients.
articles.content:
A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."
